groups.label: A · Medblocks parity
groups.kick: The seven you have to write
groups.desc: This is the set a patient-access data platform is made of. Numbered by dependency, not by difficulty — you cannot test 04 until 02 and 03 work, which is why most of the first month goes into the authorization layer.

groups.label: B · What prior authorisation forces into the core
groups.desc: These three are not in a patient-access platform and are not specific to prior auth either. Every one of them is reused by referral management, quality measure abstraction and risk adjustment. If they sit in the workflow, the second workflow re-solves them.

groups.label: C · The edge — integration, not core
groups.desc: These belong in layer 04. Nothing above them should know which one ran. When a legacy payer finally publishes a PAS endpoint, exactly one row here changes and no agent is touched.

comps.name: Source catalog & connector registry
comps.tag: A directory of every system you can connect to
comps.plain: A phone book of hospitals — and of payers. Before you can connect anything you need a list of every system and the address where its data lives.
comps.purpose: One row per connectable system: display name, vendor, FHIR base URL, the OAuth endpoints discovered from its own /.well-known/smart-configuration, the resource types read from its CapabilityStatement, and a per-vendor quirk record. Nothing is hard-coded, because every FHIR server is required to publish its endpoints at a fixed path.
build: Seed from the published lists — open.epic.com, Oracle Health, athenahealth, and the ONC Lantern dataset aggregates thousands.
Fetch /.well-known/smart-configuration per endpoint; validate it with zod before storing, so a missing token_endpoint fails at discovery rather than at 2am.
Fetch and cache /metadata once per source. Never assume a server supports a resource type — ask it.
Re-run the whole job weekly. Endpoints move, and a stale base URL looks exactly like an outage.
Trigram search over display names, because a coordinator types "Mass General", not the legal entity name.
comps.preauth: The catalog grows a second axis: payers, not just providers. A payer row records which of CRD, DTR and PAS it actually exposes, its X12 278 route through a clearinghouse, and whether it is portal-only. That single table is what lets one set of agents serve three payer capability tiers without knowing which tier they are on.

code.label: The table it fills
code.body:
CREATE TABLE sources (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  workspace_id    uuid,              -- null = shared registry row
  kind            text NOT NULL,     -- ehr | payer | clearinghouse | network | document
  display_name    text NOT NULL,
  vendor          text NOT NULL,     -- epic | oracle | athena | availity | ...
  fhir_base_url   text,
  authorize_url   text,               -- from smart-configuration
  token_url       text,
  scopes          text[],
  capabilities    jsonb,              -- from /metadata, plus crd/dtr/pas/x12 flags
  quirks          jsonb,              -- per-vendor scope strings and deviations
  discovered_at   timestamptz
);

stack: One flat catalog table. No ORM gymnastics needed.
A plain Node script against the published endpoint files.
Weekly re-discovery. Diff and alert when an endpoint moves.
Validate smart-configuration at discovery time, loudly.
Trigram similarity covers it; reach for Meilisearch only for typo tolerance.
comps.why: Two hundred lines and a cron job. There is nothing to buy here and nothing hard about it.
comps.risk: Low — but a stale endpoint is indistinguishable from an outage, so the weekly re-discovery is not optional.

comps.name: Authorization & token service
comps.tag: The hardest part to get right
comps.plain: Getting permission, and keeping it. Four different parties can grant it, and each has its own official procedure you must follow exactly.
comps.purpose: Four authorization patterns, each mapping to a published standard. Which one you use is decided by who is able to say yes, not by what is convenient. Then the unglamorous half: storing tokens encrypted and refreshing them before they expire, because refreshing after expiry is often too late and a server that rotates the refresh token on every use loses the connection permanently on a failed write.
build: Patient access — SMART standalone launch: OAuth2 authorization code with PKCE. offline_access is what gets you a refresh token; without it the connection dies at first expiry.
Clinician workflow — SMART EHR launch: your app opens inside Epic or Oracle, the EHR hands you a launch parameter carrying patient context.
Backend — SMART Backend Services: client_credentials with a signed JWT client assertion. No browser, no user, no refresh token. This is the pattern provider-side pre-auth actually runs on.
Network — Carequality / CommonWell / TEFCA: legal and organisational membership. No amount of code moves it forward. Keep it out of v1.
Proactive refresh: every few minutes, refresh anything expiring inside ten. Persist a rotated refresh token inside the same transaction that used it.
comps.preauth: Provider-side pre-auth is dominated by the backend pattern — you read on a treatment relationship under the organisation's own registration, not on per-patient consent. And the same service has to mint credentials in the other direction, outbound to payer PAS endpoints. Two directions, one token vault, one rule: an EHR's token never leaves the trust boundary that issued it. Proxy the read and re-tokenize. This is much easier to design for than to retrofit.

code.label: The backend client assertion — the grant that matters provider-side
code.body:
// Signed with your private key; the payer or EHR verifies it against your JWKS.
{
  "iss": "your-client-id",
  "sub": "your-client-id",
  "aud": "https://fhir.example-hospital.org/oauth2/token",
  "exp": 1790000300,        // under 5 minutes out
  "jti": "one-time-id"      // replay protection
}

POST /oauth2/token
  grant_type=client_credentials
  &scope=system/Patient.read system/Observation.read
  &client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
  &client_assertion=<the signed JWT>

stack: Certified Node client — discovery, PKCE, exchange, refresh. Keep a per-vendor override table for scope strings rather than patching the library.
Client assertions, and exportJWK for publishing your JWKS.
KMS signs without handing you key material. One key per environment — not one key for the whole platform.
Envelope encryption, a KMS-wrapped data key per workspace.
Holds workspace, patient, source, return URL and the PKCE verifier — server-side, never in the state parameter.
Refresh at T-10 minutes. Rotated refresh tokens written in the same transaction.
comps.effort: ≈3–4 weeks of code, months of registration
comps.why: Buy the OAuth client, write the orchestration. The multi-vendor quirk handling and the two-directional token vault are yours and nobody sells them.
comps.risk: Highest on the board. Not technically — organisationally. Production registration with each EHR vendor takes weeks to months and runs on someone else's calendar.

comps.name: Connection state machine
comps.tag: Six states, and an event on every move
comps.plain: Permission is not permanent. It can be withdrawn, and it can quietly stop working — and the system needs to know which of those happened so it can say the right thing to a human.
comps.purpose: One place owns every transition: authorizing, active, failed, refresh_failed, expired, disconnected. Each move commits the state change, an append-only audit row and an outbound event in a single transaction. Three different failures land in three different states because that is what lets you tell a revocation from an outage.
build: A Record<State, State[]> of allowed transitions and one setState() function. That is genuinely enough — reach for xstate only when guards and side effects multiply.
State change, audit row and event commit together or not at all.
Transactional outbox: write the event in the same transaction, then a poller ships it. This is what prevents the classic bug — state saved, webhook never sent.
Grant INSERT only on the audit table. No UPDATE, no DELETE. An audit log you can edit is not one.
comps.preauth: A degraded connection is not a boolean here. The evidence agent has to distinguish "no conservative-therapy documentation exists" from "the source that holds rehab notes is in refresh_failed". The first is a clinical finding; the second is an outage wearing a clinical finding's clothes. Cascade Valley's degraded source in the demo is exactly that case, and it lowers the confidence score rather than disappearing.

code.label: One place owns every transition

stack: A transition table and one function.
State, audit row and event, or nothing.
Poll-and-mark is simple and fast enough at this scale.
comps.why: Nobody sells this and it is small. Copy the lifecycle directly.
comps.risk: Low to write, high to omit. Without it, support cannot tell a customer whether their data is stale or gone.

comps.name: Retrieval engine
comps.tag: Fetching is not finished when the user is
comps.plain: Once you have permission you still have to go and collect the records, and that takes minutes or hours — long after whoever authorised it has closed the tab.
comps.purpose: After a connection goes active, schedule retrieval jobs for the resource types that source actually supports. Real servers paginate slowly, return large histories and enforce different rate limits. Two branches make the difference between a demo and a system: honouring backoff, and following Bundle.link[next].
build: A job queue per source, with per-source rate limiting. One strict vendor must not throttle every other integration.
Resource lists read from each server's CapabilityStatement, not from a constant in your code.
Follow Bundle.link[next] to the end. Without it you silently collect the first hundred records and never notice.
Exponential backoff with jitter, honouring Retry-After. Retry the same URL, never the next page.
Bulk $export for the backend pattern: kick it off, poll Content-Location, treat it as a long-running workflow rather than a request.
A pull_runs table with status, counts and errors per job. Rows for humans, traces for you.
comps.preauth: Two modes a patient-access platform never needs. First, latency-bounded reads: a CDS Hooks invocation at order-sign has roughly a five-second budget, so anything the card depends on is prefetched or asynchronous — evidence gathering cannot be a cold crawl while a clinician waits. Second, inbound subscription: the payer's decision arrives as a FHIR Subscription notification, not as something you poll for, and the same engine has to accept a push it did not schedule.

code.label: The loop, and the two branches that make it survive a real hospital

stack: BullMQ gives retries, backoff and concurrency in an afternoon. Move to Temporal when a pull spans hours and must survive a deploy.
bottleneck, or a Redis token bucket
Connection pooling matters at thousands of paged requests per pull.
Typing Bundle and link[] catches the paging mistake at compile time.
Alert on queue depth and per-source failure rate.
comps.why: The queue is bought, the crawl logic is yours. Every vendor paginates and throttles differently and that variance is the product.
comps.risk: Medium. The silent failure — collecting page one and stopping — produces confident, wrong evidence gaps.

comps.name: Clinical store — raw, then derived
comps.tag: Keep the raw truth, derive the useful shape
comps.plain: Save exactly what the source sent so you can always prove it. Then build a second, tidier copy on top that the product is actually pleasant to query.
comps.purpose: Two layers, never one. The raw table is the record you can show a regulator; the derived layer is what the agents query. Keeping a provenance pointer from derived back to raw means that when a mapping turns out to be wrong you re-derive rather than apologise. The unique key on (source, resource_type, resource_id) is what makes a re-pull idempotent.
build: raw_resources keyed UNIQUE (source_id, resource_type, resource_id), body as JSONB, upserted ON CONFLICT.
A derived clinical-domain-model layer: medications, labs, imaging, therapy episodes, problems — each carrying a provenance pointer to the raw resource it came from.
Derivation runs as a separate, idempotent job type. Never derive in place, so a corrected mapping can be replayed over history.
Patient matching: deterministic on name + date of birth + MRN first; probabilistic linkage only with a human review queue behind it.
comps.preauth: This is where a medical-necessity criterion becomes answerable. "Six weeks of documented conservative therapy" must resolve to a date-ranged query over a normalised therapy model, not a regex over free text. And the derived layer has to be able to represent a negative finding — "no TB screening exists anywhere in this record" is an answer with evidentiary weight, not a missing row. A store that can only say what it has cannot support an evidence agent.

code.label: Raw in, derived out — and the key that makes a re-pull safe

stack: Good enough for a long time, and the unique key gives idempotent re-pulls for free.
Medplum if you are a TypeScript shop; HAPI for the reference implementation; Aidbox if you would rather buy support.
Both stay out of the way of the hand-written SQL you will want for JSONB and ON CONFLICT.
Duplicates are a clinical safety problem, not a data-quality footnote.
comps.why: Adopt Medplum or HAPI for resource validation, search parameters and references — several months you would otherwise reinvent slightly wrong. Write the derived layer yourself; it is the part that is actually yours.
comps.risk: This is where the openEHR decision lands — see the note under the diagram. Getting it wrong is a rewrite, not a refactor.

comps.name: Data out — query, events, export
comps.plain: Three ways to hand records over: something asks for them, you tell something that an event happened, or you push a copy into another system automatically.
comps.purpose: A read API with keyset pagination, signed webhooks with retry and dead-lettering, and exports to a FHIR server or object storage with a per-destination watermark. The watermark is what turns a nightly full dump into a cheap delta, and keeping it per destination means one slow consumer never holds the others back.
build: Keyset (cursor) pagination, not OFFSET — offsets drift and get slow exactly when a patient has a long history.
HMAC-sign every webhook over timestamp + raw body; verify against the raw body, never the parsed object.
Retry with exponential backoff and a stable event id, so a duplicate delivery is detectable.
NDJSON exports streamed to object storage — one resource per line, never an array assembled in memory.
Update the watermark only after the destination confirms the write.
comps.preauth: The largest consumer of this API is the agent layer, and that is deliberate: every agent read goes through the same audited surface, so agents are audited by construction rather than by discipline. It is also the write-back path — the authorisation number, validity window and payer reference number going back into the EHR as a durable record, which is the part the practice actually keeps.

code.label: Sign it, and let the receiver verify against the raw body

stack: Cursor pagination. Validate at the boundary.
Or buy it from Svix if you would rather not own retries and dead-lettering.
One SDK covers S3, R2 and MinIO.
Stream rows straight to the upload.
Independent per destination so one failure never blocks the rest.
comps.why: The read API is yours. Webhook infrastructure is a solved commodity and Svix is cheaper than owning dead-letter semantics.
comps.risk: Low. The one trap is verifying a signature against a re-serialised body.

comps.name: Platform shell — tenancy, keys, audit
comps.tag: What makes the other six usable by a team
comps.plain: The account system. Somewhere for a team to keep their keys, try things safely before going live, and find out what happened when a customer says it is broken.
comps.purpose: Multi-tenant workspaces with separate sandbox and production modes, API keys, an append-only auth event log, and a dashboard that lets a non-engineer answer a support question without a database client. Every row in every table carries a workspace id, and the database enforces it rather than the application remembering to.
build: Row-level security on every table. SET LOCAL app.workspace_id once per request from the API key; then a forgotten WHERE clause leaks nothing.
API keys prefixed by environment — sk_live_… and sk_sbx_… — so a leaked key is instantly identifiable. Show once, store only a hash.
Auth event log: every authorization attempt with source, outcome, error code and timestamp. This is the table support actually reads.
A dashboard of connection states, pull history and export runs.
A typed SDK generated from your OpenAPI document, so it cannot drift from the API. Later, not v1.
comps.preauth: The workspace is the provider organisation — but two edges need designing before the first customer. A SMART launch arrives with the launching EHR as the tenant, which needs a mapping table; and a clinician who practises at two organisations needs two identities with two queues, which is common and is not modelled in this prototype. Agent memory is scoped at this boundary and it is the sharpest governance risk in the product: one organisation's outcomes must never inform another's without an explicit agreement.

code.label: Make tenancy impossible to forget

stack: WorkOS if enterprise SSO will be asked for early — in healthcare it will be.
Store the hash, keep the environment in the prefix.
The database enforces it, not the application.
The screens are dense tables of connections, pulls and export runs.
Turn on PHI scrubbing before the first production event, not after.
Automates the collection, not the observation window.
comps.why: Buy enterprise SSO. Write the tenancy, because RLS plus an API-key-driven session variable is the only version that survives a forgotten WHERE clause.
comps.risk: Medium. Retrofitting workspace_id onto a live schema is the most tedious migration you will ever run — put it on every table from the first one.

comps.name: Terminology service
comps.plain: A translator between the code systems every source speaks differently, so a question can be asked once instead of once per hospital.
comps.purpose: $lookup, $expand and $translate over the code systems the workflow depends on. A medical-necessity criterion is, operationally, a value set — "conservative therapy" is an expansion, not a string. Without this the evidence agent matches text and is confidently wrong at the edges.
build: Load LOINC and RxNorm release tables into Postgres — both are freely redistributable — and join.
Run a terminology server for SNOMED CT subsumption: HAPI's, or Ontoserver if you would rather buy it.
Cache expansions per value set version. An expansion that changes silently changes every determination made after it.
Version every value set and record which version a case was judged against.
comps.preauth: CPT and HCPCS are the axis the payer cares about and the EHR order is expressed in; ICD-10-CM is the axis the policy is written in; SNOMED and LOINC are what the clinical record actually contains. Prior auth is the workflow that forces all four into the same query, which is precisely why this belongs in the platform and not in an agent.
stack: Freely redistributable. Load the release and join.
Needs an affiliate licence; in the US the NLM UMLS licence covers it.
Licensed content with a real per-seat cost. Settle it before you ship, not after.
A case is judged against the expansion in force on its date of service.
comps.why: Never hand-roll SNOMED subsumption. Adopt a server, own the value-set versioning on top of it.
comps.risk: Commercial, not technical. CPT licensing is a line item somebody has to own, and discovering it late is expensive.

comps.name: Form & template engine
comps.plain: The thing that renders a payer's form and fills in the answers it can already find in the record — and visibly leaves blank the ones it cannot.
comps.purpose: Render a FHIR Questionnaire, execute the CQL that prepopulates it against the clinical store, and return a QuestionnaireResponse. This is the mechanical core of Da Vinci DTR. The same engine renders intake forms and quality-measure abstraction sheets, which is the argument for it living in the platform.
build: A Questionnaire renderer with enableWhen, item groups and repeating items.
A CQL execution environment bound to the derived clinical models, with a per-expression provenance record so every prefilled answer can name its source.
A hard rule in the engine: an item the data cannot answer is returned empty and flagged, never inferred. The blank is the feature.
openEHR templates as the modelling discipline for the derived layer — archetype-governed structure, whether or not you run a full openEHR CDR underneath.
comps.preauth: DTR is the only part of the Da Vinci stack where the payer hands you executable logic. Being able to run it is the difference between a coordinator answering fourteen questions and reviewing two. The two questionnaire items left visibly empty in the demo are this engine refusing to guess.
stack: The published renderers are demo-grade; you will want control over the blank-item treatment.
The reference JS engine. Bind it to your derived models, not to raw FHIR.
Use the discipline even if you defer the CDR.
Every prefilled answer names the resource it came from, or it is not prefilled.
comps.why: CQL execution is adopted; the renderer and the prefill-provenance rule are yours and they are what a reviewer actually judges you on.
comps.risk: Medium. DTR coverage across payers in 2027 will be uneven, so the engine has to degrade to a static form gracefully.

comps.name: Policy & rules store
comps.plain: The payer's rules, turned from a PDF into something a machine can check — and versioned, because a case must be judged by the rules that were in force on the day.
comps.purpose: Each policy is a set of structured criteria with a value-set-backed definition, an effective date range, and a provenance link to the payer document it came from. A case is evaluated against the policy in force on its date of service, and that version is recorded on the case. This is the least glamorous component on the page and the highest leverage.
build: Criteria as rows, not prose: identifier, description, the value sets it expands to, the time window it requires, and whether it is satisfiable by a negative finding.
Effective-dated versions with no in-place edits. The version id is stamped onto every determination.
Ingestion pipeline: LLM extraction from the payer PDF into the criterion schema, then a human review queue. Nothing reaches the store unreviewed.
Take DTR's logic directly where the payer publishes it — clean, authoritative, and covers a fraction of payers today.
A drift monitor: re-fetch policy documents on a schedule and diff, because a silent policy change produces a run of denials nobody can explain.
comps.preauth: This is open question 12 and it decides the economics of the whole product. Manual curation is accurate, expensive and does not scale; pure LLM extraction scales and needs a QA process that is itself a product; DTR-only is clean and covers too few payers today. The realistic answer is all three, with the top fifty policies by volume curated by hand and the tail extracted and reviewed.
stack: No in-place edits. A new version is a new row.
The review queue is the product, not the model.
A criterion references a value set version; it does not inline codes.
Policy changes silently, and denials arrive three weeks later.
comps.why: There is nothing to buy. The curated policy pack is the second compounding asset after agent memory, and it is the one a competitor cannot copy from your marketing site.
comps.risk: Highest ongoing cost in the system. Budget it as an operations function, not a project.

comps.name: Payer edge connectors
comps.plain: Three completely different ways to reach a payer, hidden behind one interface so nothing above cares which was used.
comps.purpose: Tier 1 speaks Da Vinci PAS over FHIR with decisions pushed by Subscription. Tier 2 speaks X12 278/275/277 through a clearinghouse. Tier 3 has no machine interface at all and is reached by supervised browser automation or fax. One interface upward; three implementations downward.
build: PAS: Claim/$submit, ClaimResponse, and a Subscription endpoint for the decision push.
X12: buy the clearinghouse connection. Never build an X12 stack for 278.
Portal: per-payer scripts, change detection, and a human in the loop on every submission. Brittle by nature.
A capability record per payer in the source catalog, so routing is data rather than a conditional.
comps.preauth: The agents are identical across all three tiers. That is the whole argument for the integration layer sitting in the platform rather than inside the workflow — when a legacy payer finally publishes a PAS endpoint, one catalog row changes and no agent is touched.
stack: Inferno-test against each payer before go-live.
Buy. Enrollment per payer takes days to weeks.
Or refuse the segment. Decide deliberately.
comps.effort: ≈6 weeks for tier 1+2, ongoing for tier 3
comps.decide: buy X12, build PAS, decide on portal
comps.why: Not core. It changes per payer and per year, which is exactly the property core services must not have.
comps.risk: Portal automation breaks on every payer UI change and is the only route to a large share of payers today.

comps.name: EHR write-back & document ingestion
comps.tag: The result has to land where the practice looks
comps.plain: Putting the answer back into the chart, and reading the faxes and scans that never arrived as data in the first place.
comps.purpose: Write the authorisation number, validity window and payer reference back into the EHR as a durable record, and ingest the outside records that arrive as PDFs and faxes. Both directions are vendor-specific and both are unglamorous.
build: Write-back per vendor: DocumentReference, Task or a vendor-specific extension. Confirm which resources each customer's EHR actually accepts before promising it.
Document ingestion: OCR, classification and extraction into the derived layer, with the original always retained.
Every extracted value carries a provenance pointer to the page it came from.
comps.preauth: An approval that lives only in your dashboard is an approval the scheduler will not find. Write-back is what stops the product from becoming a second system staff have to remember to check.
stack: Scope negotiation per site. Slower than it sounds.
Buy. Retain the original alongside every extraction.
Misfiled outside records are a clinical safety issue.
comps.why: Thin per-vendor adapters over the same internal interface. The OCR itself is a commodity.
comps.risk: Write scopes are negotiated per site and are frequently the last thing a hospital IT department will grant.
